sentences.text: Stenonychosaurus is a disputed genus of troodontid dinosaur with the meaning "narrow claw lizard", named by Charles Mortram Sternberg in 1932.
This small dinosaur reached up to 2.5 meters in length and weighed about 35 kilograms, though other estimates suggest it stood 0.9 meters tall and measured between 2.4 and 3.5 meters.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — possesses an enlarged claw on the second toe, a feature characteristic of early paravian dinosaurs.
Paleontologist Dale Russell hypothesized that if Stenonychosaurus had evolved further, its brain case could have reached 1100 cm³, comparable to a human.
The species was originally described based on a foot, hand fragments, and tail vertebrae from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta.

A more complete skeleton was described by Dale Russell in 1969, forming the basis for a famous life-sized sculpture and becoming a very well-known theropod in the 1980s when its feet and cranial box were described in more detail.
The jaws joined in a wide U-shaped symphysis similar to that of an iguana, a lizard adapted to a herbivorous lifestyle.
Stenonychosaurus possessed semi-manipulative fingers capable of grasping objects and binocular vision.
Stenonychosaurus possessed very long, slender hind limbs that suggest it was capable of running quickly.
The dinosaur had bony cristae supporting its tympanic membranes, which were ossified in at least the top and bottom regions.
Growth ring counts suggest that Stenonychosaurus reached its adult size in approximately 3 to 5 years.
Historically, Stenonychosaurus was grouped with Saurornithoides in the family Saurornithoididae.
Fossils are found in the Late Cretaceous Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, and possibly the Two Medicine Formation.
It is debated whether the evolutionary trajectory of Stenonychosaurus would have led to human-like intelligence, with critics arguing such a scenario is overly anthropomorphic.
A later analysis found that the type of parental care in troodonts cannot be determined using the conventional allometric methods used by Varricchio et al.
